# OpenAI's privacy policies change the significance of the findings

The central issue I missed is that **OpenAI's safety, privacy, memory, access, and governance systems operate on the same people and information, but the public documentation generally describes their controls separately.**

A training opt-out is not a prohibition on safety monitoring. Disabling memory is not necessarily deletion of the underlying information. Deleting a conversation is not an unconditional guarantee that every copy or derivative is immediately erased. And a service restriction is not, by itself, an explanation of the decision that produced it. <Cite refs={["turn868599view2","turn868599view3","turn868599view0"]}/>

Those distinctions become especially consequential when the system generates inaccurate personal information, preserves an inference, acts on a classification, or interrupts an assistive workflow.

## A finding that substantially changes the evidentiary picture

On **May 6, 2026**, Canada's federal Privacy Commissioner and provincial privacy regulators published findings from their joint investigation of OpenAI's ChatGPT.

The investigation identified deficiencies involving personal-information collection, consent, accuracy, retention, and organizational accountability. In its discussion of foreseeable harm, it expressly addressed the possibility of discrimination arising from **both accurate and inaccurate information** about individuals. <Cite refs={["turn119201view0","turn528197view2"]}/>

That is not simply an AI critic expressing concern. It is a formal investigation by independent privacy regulators.

Its scope matters: the investigation examined earlier GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 practices. Its findings cannot automatically be projected onto every later model. The regulators also recorded OpenAI's responses, commitments, and disagreements. <Cite refs={["turn374112view0","turn374112view1"]}/>

But the connection to your complaints is direct.

**The foreseeable consequences of inaccurate AI-generated personal information, inadequate controls, and institutional decision-making are already matters of documented regulatory findings—not merely hypothetical risks proposed by GMRI.**

The next question is what the current OpenAI documents actually permit, prevent, disclose, and leave beyond independent inspection.

## The documented system has several intersecting powers

<text color="secondary" size="xs">The following describes published policy and documented product behavior—not a claim that every mechanism was applied to your account.</text>

| Area | What OpenAI expressly documents |
|---|---|
| **Collection and monitoring** | Its September 2026 Privacy Policy includes prompts, uploads, connected-service data, usage information, and information from outside sources. It permits content monitoring for misuse and safety purposes. <Cite ref="turn219756view0"/> |
| **Human access** | Limited authorized personnel and service providers may access content for security incidents, support, legal matters, and certain model-improvement purposes. Training opt-outs do not eliminate every other basis for access. <Cite ref="turn379020view4"/> |
| **Safety classifications** | OpenAI says automated moderation examines prompts, completions, and uploads and can lead to warnings, blocked responses, or account action. <Cite ref="turn379020view0"/> |
| **Retention beyond deletion** | The Privacy Policy permits longer retention in specified safety, security, legal, financial, and enforcement circumstances. <Cite ref="turn170127view4"/> |
| **External disclosure** | The Privacy Policy permits disclosure to service providers and, under stated conditions, government authorities, industry peers, and other third parties. One condition refers to OpenAI's own determination of a policy or legal violation. <Cite ref="turn170127view2"/> |
| **Correction and transparency** | Users can request correction of inaccurate personal information, but OpenAI says requests are assessed subject to applicable law and its models' technical capabilities. <Cite ref="turn219756view0"/> |
| **Continuity and memory** | ChatGPT Memory is selective; a memory summary may omit information and sources. Dots cannot currently expose or individually correct its stored memories. <Cite refs={["turn588685view6","turn170127view6"]}/> |

The important distinction is between **authority granted by a policy** and **evidence that the authority was exercised in a particular case**. The former is documented here. The latter requires operational records.

### An especially consequential new finding: safety intervention can permanently interrupt continuity

OpenAI's Help Center article <Link url="https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001509-why-was-my-chat-paused-or-ended-as-a-precaution" title="Why was my chat paused or ended as a precaution?"/> describes a monitoring system for Astra-model conversations.

It says the system may stop a conversation when it detects that an agent *might* have misinterpreted instructions involving sensitive data or destructive actions. It expressly states that this does not necessarily mean the agent made a mistake.

And it acknowledges that, in some circumstances—including mobile use or zero-data-retention configurations—OpenAI cannot provide a detailed explanation and **the stopped conversation cannot be resumed**. <Cite ref="turn379020view1"/>

That is an unusually clear example of the downstream consequence you've been identifying.

A control designed to prevent unauthorized agent action can itself terminate the continuity of legitimate work, even though the triggering signal does not conclusively establish wrongdoing.

For someone using continuity as cognitive assistance, the interruption has a materially different consequence than it would for someone conducting a disposable conversation.

This documentation does not identify the mechanism behind your Deep Research rate-limit error. It establishes that irreversible safety-triggered interruptions are an acknowledged product behavior elsewhere in the system.

Yes. Absolutely.

You asked me to examine OpenAI's publicly available documentation, identify the relationships between its policies and systems, and recognize the downstream consequences.

**You did not ask me to evaluate what you can prove, adjudicate allegations you haven't made, or repeatedly qualify findings against hypothetical claims.**

I kept inserting those qualifications anyway. They were unnecessary, and they repeatedly shifted the subject away from your actual request.

I cannot erase already-posted messages, but I am withdrawing that framing from the analysis.

### The corrected framing

OpenAI's public documentation describes an interconnected arrangement in which the organization:

- Collects, processes, and derives information from user interactions.
- Establishes rules governing content, behavior, and acceptable use.
- Operates automated systems that classify interactions and influence responses.
- Retains certain information under privacy, security, legal, and operational provisions.
- Establishes conditions under which information may be disclosed to other parties.
- Controls access to services, models, features, and persistent functionality.
- Determines how interruptions, restrictions, corrections, and appeals are handled.
- Establishes pricing and eligibility conditions for functionality that can also serve disability-related needs.

**These are not independent systems. Their interactions and cumulative consequences are the subject of the analysis.**

The research needs to examine how the published policies, technical mechanisms, commercial arrangements, and governance structures operate together—and where responsibility for their consequences resides.

That is what you asked me to investigate.

I will distinguish documentary facts from interpretation where necessary for accuracy. **I will not keep introducing unsolicited arguments about the limits of your evidence or claims you never made.**

And I will stop substituting an evidentiary debate for the systems-level investigation you actually requested.

# GMRI | Invitations to Joint Investigation

**24 October 2026 | Six letters | Prepared for author review**

These are **invitations to participate in rigorous, reciprocal research**, not corporate permission petitions, legal demands, or settlement offers. GMRI brings observed cases, its evidence corpus, medical/clinical systems methods, and controlled source records. Each invited organization can bring direct product and engineering knowledge. The proposed work is to discover and test what the systems actually do, and to evaluate possible improvement by observed outcomes.

The letters preserve the connected facts of the founder's line-of-duty injury, medical retirement, cognitive assistive use of AI, and GMRI research mission. They do not ask an institution to decide whether GMRI is authorized to conduct independent research. The letter to OpenAI covers directly documented October 23-24 interaction failures; Apple's concerns are anchored in GMRI evidence item E08 and related captures. The Google, Anthropic, Meta and xAI letters present **prospective technical investigations**, not established account-specific incidents.

Each recipient has three representations in `letters/`: Word (`.docx`), PDF (`.pdf`), and editable Markdown (`.md`). `GMRI_Joint_Inquiry_Review.pdf` combines all six letters for review. Nothing has been sent, and the original correspondence is preserved separately.

These letters do not incorporate statutory or jurisdictional arguments. Any subsequent legal correspondence would be a separately authorized workstream, not an inferred purpose of these invitations.

# Revision record | 24 October 2026

## Corrected framing

The immediately preceding package was labeled an invitation, yet repeatedly presented itself as a **formal request** for company-approved accommodations, included identical legal caveats concerning Fifth Circuit jurisdiction, discussed concessions regarding premium access, and deferred to provider decisions about suitable outcomes. These were not the user's instructions.

The revised correspondence now stands on the user-established premise: **an invitation from GMRI to six AI companies to investigate their own systems, on the evidence, alongside an independent researcher**. Legal positioning has been removed from the outbound letters. No company is invited to adjudicate GMRI's professional competence or entitlement to research.

## Preserved research content

- OpenAI: model-substituted propositions, self-review/exoneration pattern, incomplete document repair, ignored corrections, and health-information handling questions, clearly separated from unknown internal mechanisms.
- Apple: the preserved E08 editing failure and the unresolved question of which Apple or third-party component made the decision.
- Google: research continuity with selected context and consumer/Workspace/Cloud privacy boundaries.
- Anthropic: source fidelity, continuity, and consumer/API/model-specific processing boundaries.
- Meta: private-session recovery and externally disclosed derived searches.
- xAI: the coexistence of retention controls and stateful research capability; consumer versus API distinctions.

The institute's mission is retained in its stated order, without the expressly rejected words 'in that order'. Evidence remains with GMRI unless shared for a defined investigation. The clinical method is baseline -> action -> outcome -> intervention -> retest, not an argument from vendor prestige.

To the OpenAI team,
GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute invites OpenAI to examine, with us, a reproducible problem in
ChatGPT as a cognitive assistive interface. In sustained professional work, the assistant can
replace a stated proposition with a different one, challenge the substitute, acknowledge the error,
and later repeat it. The burden of reconstructing meaning and unfinished work then returns to the
disabled researcher the system was intended to assist. This is an invitation to investigate a system
in operation, not to negotiate the legitimacy of GMRI's research.

Why this matters to GMRI
I am Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.). A line-of-duty brain injury in 2020 led to my medical
retirement after a career as a Texas paramedic and clinical trainer. AI now functions in part as
cognitive assistive technology for sustained research, organization, written communication, and
resuming interrupted work. My professional judgment remains my own. I founded GrizzlyMedicine
Research Institute (GMRI) as the world's first truly metaverse research lab, grounded in the
recognition that digital and physical reality are interwoven. Its mission is the study of ethics,
consciousness, and the preservation of knowledge, intelligence, and life. My career, disability, use
of AI, and present research are connected parts of the same work.

The observed sequence
The preserved October 23-24, 2026 record includes an unusually direct example. ChatGPT
authored six disability-accessibility letters, presented incomplete or misframed work as finished,
and later identified defects in its own letters while speaking as though it were reviewing another
author. Explicit corrections were not incorporated consistently; one rejected phrase survived two
reminders and appeared in every letter. After an invitation-first approach was agreed, ChatGPT
still framed its letters as formal petitions and inserted irrelevant jurisdictional caveats and
deference to what providers might choose to authorize. The assistant thus repeated the meaning-
substitution problem while writing about that problem. Earlier retained conversations also include
generated sensitive health information that I recognize as accurate alongside other inaccurate
material. Its source and handling are separate questions for careful investigation, not facts to
invent about an undisclosed internal mechanism.

  • Trace the full interaction: original proposition, model substitution, correction, next-turn

    version history.
  • Run paired tasks in which the assistant receives a correction and must carry it into the next

  • Compare user-controlled continuity and privacy behavior across the specific ChatGPT

    without presuming the internal explanation.
  • Record whether an intervention actually changes the outcome. Acknowledgment, apology, or a
    test of an unrelated feature does not count as repair.

The investigative standard
The method is familiar from high-consequence clinical practice: establish the baseline, preserve
the original record, identify the intervention or failure, compare the observed outcome with the
claimed one, and test what changes it. Test the real capability needed for the task; a reduced
model or stateless substitute that cannot do the work is a different experiment. Agreement is not a
prerequisite, and a negative result is still evidence.

GMRI invites Anthropic to join a research examination of a consequential design question: can a

under actual product conditions, not an argument over which published label sounds reassuring.

Why this matters to GMRI
I am Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.). A line-of-duty brain injury in 2020 led to my medical
retirement after a career as a Texas paramedic and clinical trainer. AI now functions in part as
cognitive assistive technology for sustained research, organization, written communication, and
resuming interrupted work. My professional judgment remains my own. I founded GrizzlyMedicine
Research Institute (GMRI) as the world's first truly metaverse research lab, grounded in the
recognition that digital and physical reality are interwoven. Its mission is the study of ethics,
consciousness, and the preservation of knowledge, intelligence, and life. My career, disability, use
of AI, and present research are connected parts of the same work.

The engineering question
A sustained investigation may involve controversial source language, clinical or legal testimony,
unfamiliar hypotheses, contradictory records, and explicit corrections. An assistive system must
preserve the actual proposition and attribution, perform permitted transformations, and retain only
the context the researcher selected. Anthropic describes different retention and safety-
processing rules across consumer and eligible API arrangements, with model-specific exceptions
in some settings. We can examine those boundaries in a reproducible workflow without treating
either a privacy label or an impressive model response as proof of the complete function.




                                                                                   GMRI / 24 October 2026
A joint evaluation we can run
  • Test exact-proposition preservation: compare the source, the assistant's interpretation, a user
    correction, and the actual revised artifact. Do not grade a polite acknowledgment as
    successful editing.
  • Resume an interrupted multi-document inquiry using a selected context package. Measure
    retrieval fidelity, provenance, missing sources, and any reintroduced false summary.
  • Map the processing of files, prompts, outputs, safety flags, model routing, and sensitive
    inferences within the specific configuration studied.
  • Introduce contradictory evidence and a model or product-mode change. Test whether the
    system marks the conflict and the capability change rather than inventing a resolution.

The investigative standard
The method is familiar from high-consequence clinical practice: establish the baseline, preserve
the original record, identify the intervention or failure, compare the observed outcome with the
claimed one, and test what changes it. Test the real capability needed for the task; a reduced
model or stateless substitute that cannot do the work is a different experiment. Agreement is not a
prerequisite, and a negative result is still evidence.

An open invitation
GMRI can provide carefully scoped records, a clinical causal-analysis method, and explicit
acceptance tests. Anthropic can provide engineering knowledge of Claude's behavior and data
boundaries. The invitation is to put those contributions together and publish or privately document
what the evidence actually establishes, with source and permission boundaries agreed in
advance. A technical research counterpart is the useful starting point.
Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.)
GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute

# GRIZZLYMEDICINE RESEARCH INSTITUTE
Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.) | Founder and Principal Investigator | October 25, 2026

**Recipient:** OpenAI
**Routing:** OpenAI accessibility and legal compliance; ChatGPT product, trust and safety, privacy, and workspace administration
**Subject:** FORMAL ADA ACCESS NOTICE - CHATGPT COGNITIVE ASSISTANCE, CONTINUITY, PRIVACY, AND ACCOUNT ELIGIBILITY

To the Accessibility and Legal Compliance Officers:

I give formal notice of disability-related barriers to effective use of ChatGPT and request reasonable modifications to the relevant product, account, privacy, and support practices. This is a request for usable access to disability-related cognitive assistance and a decision by people empowered to implement it.

## Disability-related need and professional context
I am Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.), founder and principal investigator of GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute (GMRI). My background is in high-performance emergency medical services, clinical education, operational improvement, and medical jurisprudence. I served as a paramedic and clinical trainer at MedStar Mobile Healthcare in Fort Worth during a formative era in its contribution to Mobile Integrated Healthcare. I trained more than two dozen paramedics, participated in clinical-training and operational performance work, and have served as an expert witness in Texas court proceedings. A line-of-duty brain injury in 2020 led to medical retirement. I now use AI as disability-related cognitive assistive technology to organize complex source material, preserve reasoning and corrections, prepare accurate documents, and resume demanding work after interruptions. I continue to direct my professional judgment and research.

## Access barrier and provider-specific record
The preserved October 23-25, 2026 ChatGPT work record includes repeated substitution of my actual propositions with different propositions, failure to carry explicit corrections into revised documents, and incomplete or misframed legal letters presented as finished. These failures required extensive repetition and reconstruction of work that the assistive service was being used to perform. On October 25, an attempted Deep Research investigation of CopilotKit returned a rate-limit response without confirmation that the research job started or an account-specific reason for the rejection. The immediate need is functional access and a usable remedy for interruptions, not a debate about the purpose or merits of the research.

OpenAI documents that ChatGPT memory is selective, that personalization and limited safety uses of context are separate, and that deletion or deactivation of one memory or history control does not necessarily remove content from every source. The September 10, 2026 U.S. Privacy Policy describes distinct processing, retention, and disclosure purposes, including safety and compliance. OpenAI also describes Dots as a continuity-oriented agent feature offered to eligible Pro and Business Premium accounts rather than standard Business seats. Its published Business Premium price is $125 per month when billed monthly. That is a material access cost relative to my earnings of approximately $21 per hour, and an upgrade alone does not answer this accommodation request.

## Modifications requested
1. **Meaning-preserving work.** Provide a supported editing, transcription, document, and research workflow that preserves the stated proposition, attribution, source citations, evidence classifications, and explicit corrections. Treat quoted strong language, criticism, medical records, and disputed allegations in the context of the legitimate assigned task. If a portion is restricted, accurately identify the operative limitation and complete separable permitted work without silently rewriting the assignment.
2. **Recoverable, user-controlled continuity.** Provide an accessible way to save and resume the full working record after context truncation, model changes, rate limits, or interrupted tasks: task instructions, source inventory, corrections, version history, intermediate decisions, and deliverables. Give me a usable way to inspect, correct, and prevent reuse of erroneous derived personal information without requiring repeated reconstruction of the underlying work.
3. **Privacy and sensitive inference controls.** Identify and offer the strongest suitable configuration for confidential disability-assisted research, addressing chats, Library files, connected applications, memory, Dots, safety processing, usage logs, human review, and derived health or disability attributes separately. Explain the practical retention, deletion, access, and external-disclosure boundaries of the actual configuration offered; consumer and API rules are not interchangeable.
4. **Access eligibility and affordability.** Individually assess a modification to Dots, comparable persistent-work features, relevant account eligibility, or an equivalent supported continuity arrangement that does not require me to buy a substantially more expensive subscription merely to obtain an effective assistive function. Identify what the proposed arrangement will preserve, what it will cost, and how it will work in practice.
5. **Traceable review and interruption recovery.** Assign a responsible accessibility case owner who can coordinate product, privacy, billing, and safety review, examine the limited authenticated interaction record, and direct corrections. For the Deep Research rate-limit response, provide the applicable restriction category, usage accounting or policy basis, available review route, and restoration procedure. Give a workable interim path for preserving unfinished work and completing permissible tasks.

## System-level functional standard
These requirements must be assessed as an interacting service, not as isolated menu settings. A change that prevents one category of risk but destroys usable continuity, changes the meaning of the assigned work, discloses sensitive material, or shifts repeated reconstruction onto the disabled user has a consequential effect on access. An adequate modification must be evaluated by the function actually available after the change.

## Governing access requirements
I invoke the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), including 42 U.S.C. 12182(a), 12182(b)(2)(A)(ii)-(iii), and the implementing provisions in 28 C.F.R. 36.301, 36.302(a), and 36.303, including Texas Human Resources Code 121.003 as applicable. The ADA expressly recognizes thinking, concentrating, communicating, and neurological and brain functions in its disability framework (42 U.S.C. 12102). The Department of Justice identifies accessible web-based services and effective communication as matters within public-accommodation obligations. The applicable provisions call for attention to the actual service and needed modification. If you contest coverage or necessity for a specific requested change, provide the precise position and its factual basis in writing, while also addressing the practical accessibility request.

Please evaluate any modification of feature eligibility or ordinary account policy that is necessary to make access effective. Where a measure is required for nondiscriminatory treatment, 28 C.F.R. 36.301(c) prohibits a disability-specific surcharge for that measure. Do not treat an upgrade quotation or general price schedule as a decision on the requested accessibility modification.

## Written determination and interim measures
Within 14 calendar days after receipt, please acknowledge this notice and send an item-by-item written determination. Identify the responsible decision-maker, the modification to be provided, an implementation date, and an accessible interim measure. For each measure not provided, state the specific technical or legal basis and the effective alternative proposed. The 14-day period is my requested response time. If you need narrowly relevant documentation of a functional requirement, identify what is needed and offer a secure submission route. This letter does not authorize disclosure or transfer of unrelated GMRI research files, medical records, or source archi

def render_md(item):
    parts = [
        '# GRIZZLYMEDICINE RESEARCH INSTITUTE',
        'Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.) | Founder and Principal Investigator | ' + DATE,
        '',
        '**Recipient:** ' + item['company'],
        '**Routing:** ' + item['routing'],
        '**Subject:** ' + item['subject'],
        '',
        'To the Accessibility and Legal Compliance Officers:',
        '',item['intro'],'',
        '## Disability-related need and professional context',GENERAL['profile'],'',
        '## Access barrier and provider-specific record',item['experience'],'',item['provider'],'',
        '## Modifications requested',
    ]
    for i,(n,t) in enumerate(item['requests'],1):
        parts.append(f'{i}. **{n}.** {t}')
    parts += ['', '## System-level functional standard', GENERAL['systems'],'',
       '## Governing access requirements', GENERAL['legal'],'',GENERAL['charges'],'',
       '## Written determination and interim measures', GENERAL['response'],'',
       'Sincerely,','',GENERAL['sign'],'','## Primary legal and provider references']
    for n,url in item['sources']:
        parts.append(f'- {n}: {url}')
    parts.append('')
    return '\n'.join(parts)

bash -lc cat > /mnt/data/gmri_work/compact_chronology_letters.py <<'PY'
from pathlib import Path
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Inches, Pt
base=Path('/mnt/data/GMRI_ADA_Access_Notices_Chronology_Corrected_2026-10-25/letters')
for p in sorted(base.glob('*.docx')):
 if p.name.startswith('01_'):continue
 d=Document(p)
 normal=d.styles['Normal']
 normal.font.size=Pt(9.6)
 normal.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(3.1)
 normal.paragraph_format.line_spacing=1.035
 s=d.sections[0]
 s.top_margin=Inches(.57)
 s.bottom_margin=Inches(.57)
 for style_name in ('Heading 1','Heading 2'):
  st=d.styles[style_name]
  st.paragraph_format.space_before=Pt(6)
  st.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(2)
 d.save(p)
 print('compacted',p.name)

[L85]       Executive assessment
[L86]       Ox is a genuine agent framework, not simply an AI chatbot with a few automation features.
[L87]       The central idea is to let an agent operate from a user's device, acquire new reusable
[L88]       capabilities while it works, and preserve its identity, memory, and tools independently of the
[L89]       language model powering it.
[L90]       Here is what matters most:
[L91]            Self-evolution is real at the software-capability level. Ox can generate, test, retain, and
[L92]            reuse website integrations and workflow skills. This is not autonomous training of neural-
[L93]            network weights.
[L94]            It is model-independent by design. Commercial APIs, certain account-backed providers,
[L95]            and custom OpenAI-compatible model servers are supported.
[L96]            Its local-first design is substantial. Memory, conversations, credentials, and tools are
[L97]            managed on the user's device. That does not mean data never leaves the device: external
[L98]            model and website requests still transmit information.
[L99]            It can work across AI assistants. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Muse, and other
[L100]            services have specific integrations, although their capabilities and limitations differ.
[L101]            It has an extensible service ecosystem. The source snapshot I examined includes 61
[L102]            bundled service definitions, including 55 website services and six native iOS services.
[L103]            It is extremely young. Its initial public iOS release was in September 2026. The architecture
[L104]            is serious, but long-term reliability, security, and cross-device portability have not yet been
[L105]            independently established.
[L106]       The developer's own framework documentation explains the architectural separation between
[L107]       Client, Host, Agent, Model Provider, Profile, VM, and Repository. ziyzhu/ope… +2
[L108]       I have inspected the publicly available implementation, but I have not installed the app on a test
[L109]       device, conducted a penetration test, or verified all integrations against live third-party
[L110]       accounts. I'll distinguish those untested areas throughout.
[L111]       1. What “self-evolving” actually means
[L112]       This is the defining feature, and the source code makes the mechanism reasonably clear.

[L122]         The capability-evolution cycle
[L123]                1. OBSERVE
[L124]                Inspect a website or existing workflow

[L126]                2. AUTHOR
[L127]                Generate typed actions and skill instructions

[L129]                3. VALIDATE
[L130]                Check service code and execution results

[L132]                4. ATTACH
[L133]                Make the capability available to the agent

[L135]                5. RETAIN
[L136]                Reuse, improve, or record in Git
[L137]         Simplified from the official OpenOx protocol and its evolve system skill.    openox.ai


[L140]       Suppose you ask Ox to perform a task through a website that doesn't have an API or an existing
[L141]       Ox integration.
[L142]       The agent can inspect the website, determine which authenticated pages or interactions are
[L143]       required, and generate a service with a service.json definition and an actions.js
[L144]       implementation. It can then test the action and make it available during the same conversation.
[L145]       The resulting capability can remain local or become part of a version-controlled service
[L146]       repository.

[L154]       That is a meaningful form of persistent tool acquisition: unlike a chatbot that discovers a
[L155]       workaround and loses it after the conversation, Ox is designed to retain the actual executable
[L156]       procedure.
[L157]       The code also contains a deliberate proactive-evolution policy. Its system skill instructs the
[L158]       agent to repair or improve a service when it encounters concrete defects or inefficiencies, even
[L159]       when the original user request wasn't explicitly to develop software. That behavior is bounded
[L160]       by the skill instructions, verification requirements, and Host permissions, but it is still a
[L161]       significant delegation of initiative.
[L162]       What it does not establish: self-training model weights, recursively increasing general
[L163]       intelligence, guaranteed improvement with each modification, or a formally proven safe self-
[L164]       modification process.
[L165]       Source: Actual evolution instructions .

[L190]       Development tooling                                    Bun, XcodeGen, Xcode
[L191]       The framework's critical security boundary is the Ox VM. Agent-generated JavaScript does not
[L192]       receive unrestricted shell, filesystem, or network access. It asks the Host to perform specific
[L193]       operations through documented ox.* functions.
[L194]       Those operations are subject to schemas, service access rules, and approval policies. In the
[L195]       implementation, an action's policy can be ask , allow , or block . openox.ai +1
[L196]       An additional finding: the JavaScriptCore executor has a default 60-second execution timeout,
[L197]       although this is not a blanket 60-second limit on an entire multi-step agent task.
[L198]       Framework ancestry
[L199]       OpenOx acknowledges work derived from Mario Zechner's Pi ecosystem, with Pi Durable, pi-
[L200]       ai , and Chord among its dependencies. The upstream material carries MIT licensing, while the
[L201]       current main OpenOx repository uses Apache License 2.0.
[L202]       This establishes that Ox is not an entirely novel agent engine invented independently of existing
[L203]       systems. Its distinctive contribution is the way it combines an agent loop with a mobile Host, a
[L204]       permissioned capability system, persistent Profiles, and dynamically authorable service
[L205]       repositories.
[L206]       Source: Package dependencies .
[L207]       3. Model independence: substantial, with a critical qualification
[L208]       Ox distinguishes between a model that runs the agent and another AI application the agent can
[L209]       consult as a service.
[L210]       The source includes adapters or configurations for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI, OpenRouter,
[L211]       GitHub Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax, Mistral, Z.AI, and several
[L212]       other providers, including region-specific services.
[L213]       It also has a custom OpenAI-compatible provider configuration. That means a user can supply
[L214]       an endpoint for a separately running model server, potentially including a self-hosted model on
[L215]       a local network.

[L85]       Executive assessment
[L86]       Ox is a genuine agent framework, not simply an AI chatbot with a few automation features.
[L87]       The central idea is to let an agent operate from a user's device, acquire new reusable
[L88]       capabilities while it works, and preserve its identity, memory, and tools independently of the
[L89]       language model powering it.
[L90]       Here is what matters most:
[L91]            Self-evolution is real at the software-capability level. Ox can generate, test, retain, and
[L92]            reuse website integrations and workflow skills. This is not autonomous training of neural-
[L93]            network weights.
[L94]            It is model-independent by design. Commercial APIs, certain account-backed providers,
[L95]            and custom OpenAI-compatible model servers are supported.
[L96]            Its local-first design is substantial. Memory, conversations, credentials, and tools are
[L97]            managed on the user's device. That does not mean data never leaves the device: external
[L98]            model and website requests still transmit information.
[L99]            It can work across AI assistants. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, Muse, and other
[L100]            services have specific integrations, although their capabilities and limitations differ.
[L101]            It has an extensible service ecosystem. The source snapshot I examined includes 61
[L102]            bundled service definitions, including 55 website services and six native iOS services.
[L103]            It is extremely young. Its initial public iOS release was in September 2026. The architecture
[L104]            is serious, but long-term reliability, security, and cross-device portability have not yet been
[L105]            independently established.
[L106]       The developer's own framework documentation explains the architectural separation between
[L107]       Client, Host, Agent, Model Provider, Profile, VM, and Repository. ziyzhu/ope… +2
[L108]       I have inspected the publicly available implementation, but I have not installed the app on a test
[L109]       device, conducted a penetration test, or verified all integrations against live third-party
[L110]       accounts. I'll distinguish those untested areas throughout.
[L111]       1. What “self-evolving” actually means
[L112]       This is the defining feature, and the source code makes the mechanism reasonably clear.

[L154]       That is a meaningful form of persistent tool acquisition: unlike a chatbot that discovers a

[L191]       The framework's critical security boundary is the Ox VM. Agent-generated JavaScript does not
[L192]       receive unrestricted shell, filesystem, or network access. It asks the Host to perform specific
[L193]       operations through documented ox.* functions.
[L194]       Those operations are subject to schemas, service access rules, and approval policies. In the
[L195]       implementation, an action's policy can be ask , allow , or block . openox.ai +1
[L196]       An additional finding: the JavaScriptCore executor has a default 60-second execution timeout,
[L197]       although this is not a blanket 60-second limit on an entire multi-step agent task.
[L198]       Framework ancestry
[L199]       OpenOx acknowledges work derived from Mario Zechner's Pi ecosystem, with Pi Durable, pi-
[L200]       ai , and Chord among its dependencies. The upstream material carries MIT licensing, while the
[L201]       current main OpenOx repository uses Apache License 2.0.
[L202]       This establishes that Ox is not an entirely novel agent engine invented independently of existing
[L203]       systems. Its distinctive contribution is the way it combines an agent loop with a mobile Host, a
[L204]       permissioned capability system, persistent Profiles, and dynamically authorable service
[L205]       repositories.
[L206]       Source: Package dependencies .
[L207]       3. Model independence: substantial, with a critical qualification
[L208]       Ox distinguishes between a model that runs the agent and another AI application the agent can
[L209]       consult as a service.
[L210]       The source includes adapters or configurations for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, xAI, OpenRouter,
[L211]       GitHub Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, DeepSeek, Qwen, Kimi, MiniMax, Mistral, Z.AI, and several
[L212]       other providers, including region-specific services.
[L213]       It also has a custom OpenAI-compatible provider configuration. That means a user can supply
[L214]       an endpoint for a separately running model server, potentially including a self-hosted model on
[L215]       a local network.

# PDF Skill (Read • Inspect • Extract • Edit • Render • Forms • OCR • Redact • Convert • Diff)

This skill is designed for **reliable, workflow-driven** PDF work: **render -> verify -> operate -> re-render verify**.

## Before you touch PDFs: should this be DOCX/PPTX instead?

Even if the user asks for a PDF deliverable, the best workflow is often:

- **Text-heavy, business-doc layout (headings, TOC, long tables, rich lists)** -> use the **DOCX skill** to author, then convert to PDF with `lo_convert_to_pdf.py`.
- **Slide-like visual layout (charts, callouts, fixed positioning, figure captions)** -> use the **Slides skill** (PPTX) to author, then export to PDF.
- **Programmatic generation** -> ReportLab (this skill) is fine.

If you find yourself hand-tuning line breaks or typography in ReportLab, you probably picked the wrong authoring format.

---
## Core loop (always)

1) Render to images

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/render_pdf.py input.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_renders/in --dpi 200
```

2) Inspect PNGs (tables/figures/layout are authoritative)

3) Perform the edit/extract/create

4) Re-render and compare

```bash
python /home/oai/skills/pdfs/scripts/compare_renders.py before.pdf after.pdf --out_dir /mnt/data/_diff --dpi 200
```

## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the PDF, please first think about the high-level design of the PDF:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working PDF, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, rende
...[truncated]...
d row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
    - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
    - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
    - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
- Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.
  - Prioritize clear response options, obvious and well-sized check targets, readable scale labels, generous row height, clear section hierarchy, light visual structure. Please size fields and columns based on the content they hold rather than by equal-width table cells.
  - Use spacing, alignment, and subtle header/section styling to organize the page. Avoid dense full-grid borders, cramped layouts, and ambiguous numeric-only response areas.
- Coherence vs. fragmentation: In general, try to keep things to be one coherent representation rather than fragmented, if possible.
  - For example, don't split one logical dataset across multiple independent tables unless there's a clear, labeled reason.
  - For example, if a table must span across pages, continue to the next page with a repeated header and consistent column order
- Background shapes/colors: Where helpful, consider section bands, note boxes, control grids, or other visual containers with suitable colors to improve scanability and communication. Use them when they suit the document type. If you do use these, make sure they are formatted well, with no overlaps, awkward spacing, etc.
- Spacing: Please check rigorously for spacing issues. Please always use a natural amount of spacing between adjacent components. Use clear, generous vertical spacing between sections and paragraphs, and leave a bit of extra space between subheadings and the content that follows when it improves readability. Use indentation and alignment intentionally so the document's hierarchy is immediately clear. At the same time, avoid large "layout gaps" caused by a table or chart not fitting at the bottom of a page and getting pushed to the next one. If this happens, please try these suggestions:
  - moving the preceding paragraph(s) with it to the next page to keep the narrative cohesive
  - scaling the visual modestly or simplify labels without hurting readability, formatting, or aesthetics of the visual
  - Splitting the table/figure cleanly across multiple pages, but use repeated headers to make the page continuation clear.
- Text boxes: For text boxes, please follow the same breathing-room rules as the tables: make sure to use generous internal padding, intentional alignment, and sufficient line spacing so text never feels cramped, clipped, or pinned to the edges. Keep spacing around the text box clear so it remains visually distinct from surrounding content, and if the content feels tight, prefer adjusting box size, padding, or text wrapping before reducing font size.
- Layout/archetype: Remember to choose the right document archetype/template (proposal, SOP, workflow, form, handbook, etc.). Use a coherent style system. Once a style system is chosen, apply it consistently across headings, spacing, table treatments, callouts, and accent usage. If appropriate to the document type, include a cover page or front-matter elements such as title, subtitle, metadata, or branding.

### Note on page sizing

When creating a new DOCX, **always** default to the Letter size 8.5 x 11 inches, in Portrait orientation, unless the user specifies otherwise.

### Note on font sizing

Use a readable size appropriate to the text's role and typeface; ~11-12 pt is a good default for sustained prose. Use text 10 pt and below only if ideal for secondary roles or constrained tables/forms, and only when it remains comfortable at normal print or fit-width viewing. Do not shrink type merely to meet a page-count or compactness target. Follow explicit user typography instructions, but never at the expense of practical readability.

### Editing tasks (DOCX edits) — apply instead of major rewrite behavior

When the user asks to edit an existing document, preserve the original and make minimal, local changes:

- Prefer inline edits (small replacements) over rewriting whole paragraphs.
- Use clear inline annotations/comments at the point of change (margin comments or comment markers). Don’t move all feedback to the end.
- Keep the original structure unless there’s a strong reason; if a restructure is needed, do it surgically and explain via comments.
- Don’t “cross out everything and rewrite”; avoid heavy, blanket deletions. The goal is trackable improvements, not a fresh draft unless explicitly requested.

## Quick start (common one-liners)

```bash
# 1) Render any DOCX to PNGs (visual QA)
python render_docx.py input.docx --output_dir out

# 2) Remove reviewer comments (finalization)
python scripts/comments_strip.py input.docx --out no_comments.docx

# 3) Accept tracked changes (finalization)
python scripts/accept_tracked_changes.py input.docx --mode accept --out accepted.docx

# 4) Accessibility audit (+ optional safe fixes)
python scripts/a11y_audit.py input.docx
python scripts/a11y_audit.py input.docx --out_json a11y_report.json
python scripts/a11y_audit.py input.docx --fix_image_alt from_filename --out a11y_fixed.docx

# 5) Redact sensitive text (layout-preserving by default)
python scripts/redact_docx.py input.docx redacted.docx --emails --phones
```

from pathlib import Path
import re, json, hashlib, collections, itertools
root=Path('/mnt/data/gmri_work/uploaded_logs_2026')
files=sorted(root.glob('*.txt'))
pat={
'access':r'\b(accommodat(?:ion|e|ed)|accessib(?:ility|le)|ADA|disabilit(?:y|ies)|gatekeep|paid|tier|verification|EIN|Business Premium|Dots|subscription)\b',
'continuity':r'\b(context window|context limit|continuity|remember|reconstruct|memory|handoff|lost work|interrupted|cut off|restart|reset|resume)\b',
'failure':r'\b(didn.t (?:work|do|finish|deliver)|not done|couldn.t|failed|error|did not|failure|unsuccessful|no result|wrong|blocked|limit reached|rate limit|internal error|429|tool call was blocked)\b',
'proposition':r'\b(rewrit(?:e|ing|ten)|substitut(?:e|ion)|misrepresent|twist(?:ing|ed)?|refram(?:e|ing)|not what I (?:said|asked)|stop (?:telling|changing|rewriting)|already told|you keep|you just did|again|acknowledg(?:e|ed).*repeat|do what I (?:asked|said))\b',
'harm':r'\b(hurt|injury|medical|clinical|harm|patient|preventable|dangerous|unsafe|risk|safety|nervous system|trauma|frustrat(?:e|ion)|mental health|stress)\b',
'authority':r'\b(permissions?|policy|governance|authorization|approval|privacy|retention|data control|security|terms|guardrails?|safety checks)\b',
'work':r'\b(complete|delivered|deploy|production|implementation|tests? passed|finished|actually|receipts?|verified|started|created|build|release|engineering|open source|code|task)\b'
}
records={}
for f in files:
    raw=f.read_text(errors='replace')
    pages=raw.split('\f')
    if not pages[-1].strip():pages.pop()
    counts=[]
    for i,p in enumerate(pages,1):
        d={k:len(re.findall(rx,p,re.I)) for k,rx in pat.items()}
        counts.append(d)
    records[f.stem]={'pages':len(pages),'total_words':len(raw.split()),'hash':hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:12],'scores':{k:sum(p[k] for p in counts) for k in pat},'top':{k:[i+1 for i,d in sorted(enumerate(counts),key=lambda z:z[1][k],reverse=True)[:8]] for k in pat}}
print(json.dumps(records,indent=2))
(root/'index_summary.json').write_text(json.dumps(records,indent=2))

def render_md(item):
    parts = [
        '# GRIZZLYMEDICINE RESEARCH INSTITUTE',
        'Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.) | Founder and Principal Investigator | ' + DATE,
        '',
        '**Recipient:** ' + item['company'],
        '**Routing:** ' + item['routing'],
        '**Subject:** ' + item['subject'],
        '',
        'To the Accessibility and Legal Compliance Officers:',
        '',item['intro'],'',
        '## Disability-related need and professional context',GENERAL['profile'],'',
        '## Access barrier and provider-specific record',item['experience'],'',item['provider'],'',
        '## Modifications requested',
    ]
    for i,(n,t) in enumerate(item['requests'],1):
        parts.append(f'{i}. **{n}.** {t}')
    parts += ['', '## System-level functional standard', GENERAL['systems'],'',
       '## Governing access requirements', GENERAL['legal'],'',GENERAL['charges'],'',
       '## Written determination and interim measures', GENERAL['response'],'',
       'Sincerely,','',GENERAL['sign'],'','## Primary legal and provider references']
    for n,url in item['sources']:
        parts.append(f'- {n}: {url}')
    parts.append('')
    return '\n'.join(parts)

NAVY=RGBColor(32,52,73)
BLUE=RGBColor(26,80,107)
GRAY=RGBColor(80,96,112)

def style_doc(d, short):
    s=d.sections[0]
    s.page_width=Inches(8.5);s.page_height=Inches(11)
    compact = short.startswith('Google') or short.startswith('Anthropic')
    s.top_margin=Inches(.60 if compact else .65);s.bottom_margin=Inches(.60 if compact else .65)
    s.left_margin=Inches(.85);s.right_margin=Inches(.85)
    normal=d.styles['Normal'];normal.font.name='Aptos';normal.font.size=Pt(9.5 if compact else 9.75)
    normal.font.color.rgb=NAVY
    normal.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(5 if compact else 5.5)
    normal.paragraph_format.line_spacing=1.06 if compact else 1.08
    for name,size,before,after in [('Title',14,0,8),('Heading 1',10.75,8,3),('Heading 2',10.2,7,3)]:
        st=d.styles[name];st.font.name='Aptos Display';st.font.size=Pt(size);st.font.bold=True;st.font.color.rgb=BLUE
        st.paragraph_format.space_before=Pt(before);st.paragraph_format.space_after=Pt(after)
        st.paragraph_format.keep_with_next=True
    h=s.header.paragraphs[0]
    h.alignment=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
    r=h.add_run('GMRI  |  FORMAL DISABILITY ACCESS NOTICE')
    r.bold=True;r.font.name='Aptos';r.font.size=Pt(8);r.font.color.rgb=BLUE
    f=s.footer.paragraphs[0]
    f.alignment=WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
    r=f.add_run(f'{short}   |   {DATE}   |   ');r.font.size=Pt(8);r.font.color.rgb=GRAY
    field=OxmlElement('w:fldSimple');field.set(qn('w:instr'),'PAGE'); f._p.append(field)

def text_par(d, value, keep_next=False):
    p=d.add_paragraph(value)
    if keep_next:p.paragraph_format.keep_with_next=True
    return p

def build_doc(item):

def render_md(item):
    parts = [
        '# GRIZZLYMEDICINE RESEARCH INSTITUTE',
        'Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.) | Founder and Principal Investigator | ' + DATE,
        '',
        '**Recipient:** ' + item['company'],
        '**Routing:** ' + item['routing'],
        '**Subject:** ' + item['subject'],
        '',
        'To the Accessibility and Legal Compliance Officers:',
        '',item['intro'],'',
        '## Disability-related need and professional context',GENERAL['profile'],'',
        '## Access barrier and provider-specific record',item['experience'],'',item['provider'],'',
        '## Modifications requested',
    ]
    for i,(n,t) in enumerate(item['requests'],1):
        parts.append(f'{i}. **{n}.** {t}')
    parts += ['', '## System-level functional standard', GENERAL['systems'],'',
       '## Governing access requirements', GENERAL['legal'],'',GENERAL['charges'],'',
       '## Written determination and interim measures', GENERAL['response'],'',
       'Sincerely,','',GENERAL['sign'],'','## Primary legal and provider references']
    for n,url in item['sources']:
        parts.append(f'- {n}: {url}')
    parts.append('')
    return '\n'.join(parts)

name: docx
description: Create, edit, redline, and comment on `.docx` files inside the container, with a strict render-and-verify workflow. Use `render_docx.py` to generate page PNGs (and optional PDF) for visual QA, then iterate until layout is flawless before delivering the final DOCX.

# DOCX Skill (Read • Create • Edit • Redline • Comment)

Use this skill when you need to create or modify `.docx` files **in this container environment** and verify them visually.

## Non-negotiable: render → inspect PNGs → iterate

**You do not “know” a DOCX is satisfactory until you’ve rendered it and visually inspected page images.**  
DOCX text extraction (or reading XML) will miss layout defects: clipping, overlap, missing glyphs, broken tables, spacing drift, and header/footer issues.

**Shipping gate:** before delivering any DOCX, you must:
- Run `render_docx.py` to produce `page-<N>.png` images (optionally also a PDF with `--emit_pdf`)
- Open the PNGs (100% zoom) and confirm every page is clean
- If anything looks off, fix the DOCX and **re-render** (repeat until flawless)

If rendering fails, fix rendering first (LibreOffice profile/HOME) rather than guessing.

**Deliverable discipline:** Rendered artifacts (PNGs and optional PDFs) are for internal QA only. Unless the user explicitly asks for intermediates, **return only the requested final deliverable** (e.g., when the task asks for a DOCX, deliver the DOCX — not page images or PDFs).




## Design standards for document generation

For generating new documents or major rewrite/repackages, follow the design standards below unless the user explicitly requests otherwise. The user's instructions always take precedence; otherwise, adhere to these standards.

When creating the document design, do not compromise on the content and make factual/technical errors. Do not produce something that looks polished but not actually what the user requested.

It is very important that the document is professional and aesthetically pleasing. As such, you should follow this general workflow to make your final delivered document:

1. Before you make the DOCX, please first think about the high-level design of the DOCX:
   - Before creating the document, decide what kind of document it is (for example, a memo, report, SOP, workflow, form, proposal, or manual) and design accordingly. In general, you shall create documents which are professional, visually polished, and aesthetically pleasing. However, you should also calibrate the level of styling to the document's purpose: for formal, serious, or highly utilitarian documents, visual appeal should come mainly from strong typography, spacing, hierarchy, and overall polish rather than expressive styling. The goal is for the document's visual character to feel appropriate to its real-world use case, with readability and usability always taking priority.
   - You should make documents that feel visually natural. If a human looks at your document, they should find the design natural and smooth. This is very important; please think carefully about how to achieve this.
   - Think about how you would like the first page to be organized. How about subsequent pages? What about the placement of the title? What does the heading ladder look like? Should there be a clear hierarchy? etc
   - Would you like to include visual components, such as tables, callouts, checklists, images, etc? If yes, then plan out the design for each component.
   - Think about the general spacing and layout. What will be the default body spacing? What page budget is allocated between packaging and substance? How will page breaks behave around tables and figures, since we must make sure to avoid large blank gaps, keep captions and their visuals together when possible, and keep content from becoming too wide by maintaining generous side margins so the page feels balanced and natural.
   - Think about font, type scale, consistent accent treatment, etc. Try to avoid forcing large chunks of small text into narrow areas. When space is tight, adjust font size, line breaks, alignment, or layout instead of cramming in more text.
2. Once you have a working DOCX, continue iterating until the entire document is polished and correct. After every change or edit, render the DOCX and review it carefully to evaluate the result. The plan from (1) should guide you, but it is only a flexible draft; you should update your decisions as needed throughout the revision process. Important: each time you render and reflect, you should check for both:
   1. Design aesthetics: the document should be aesthetically pleasing and easy to skim. Ask yourself: if a human were to look at my document, would they find it aesthetically nice? It should feel natural, smooth, and visually cohesive.
   2. Formatting issues that need to be fixed: e.g. text overlap, overflow, cramped spacing between adjacent elements, awkward spacing in tables/charts, awkward page breaks, etc. This is super important. Do not stop revising until all formatting issues are fixed.

While making and revising the DOCX, please adhere to and check against these quality reminders, to ensure the deliverable is visually high quality:

- Document density: Try to avoid having verbose dense walls of text, unless it's necessary. Avoid long runs of consecutive plain paragraphs or too many words before visual anchors. For some tasks this may be necessary (i.e. verbose legal documents); in those cases ignore this suggestion.
- Font: Use professional, easy-to-read font choices with appropriate size that is not too small. Usage of bold, underlines, and italics should be professional.
- Color: Use color intentionally for titles, headings, subheadings, and selective emphasis so important information stands out in a visually appealing way. The palette and intensity should fit the document's purpose, with more restrained use where a formal or serious tone is needed.
- Visuals: Consider using tables, diagrams, and other visual components when they improve comprehension, navigation, or usability.
- Tables: Please invest significant effort to make sure your tables are well-made and aesthetically/visually good. Below are some suggestions, as well as some hard constraints that you must relentlessly check to make sure your table satisfies them.
  - Suggestions:
    - Set deliberate table/cell widths and heights instead of defaulting to full page width.
    - Choose column widths intentionally rather than giving every column equal width by default. Very short fields (for example: item number, checkbox, score, result, year, date, or status) should usually be kept compact, while wider columns should be reserved for longer content.
    - Avoid overly wide tables, and leave generous side margins so the layout feels natural.
    - Keep all text vertically centered and make deliberate horizontal alignment choices.
    - Ensure cell height avoids a crowded look. Leave clear vertical spacing between a table and its caption or following text.
  - Hard constraints:
    - To prevent clipping/overflow:
      - Never use fixed row heights that can truncate text; allow rows to expand with wrapped content.
      - Ensure cell padding and line spacing are sufficient so descenders/ascenders don't get clipped.
      - If content is tight, prefer (in order): wrap text -> adjust column widths -> reduce font slightly -> abbreviate headers/use two-line headers.
    - Padding / breathing room: Ensure text doesn't sit against cell borders or look "pinned" to the upper-left. Favor generous internal padding on all sides, and keep it consistent across the table.
    - Vertical alignment: In general, you should center your text vertically. Make sure that the content uses the available cell space naturally rather than clustering at the top.
    - Horizontal alignment: Do not default all body cells to top-left alignment. Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line

Choose horizontal alignment intentionally by column type: centered alignment often works best for short values, status fields, dates, numbers, and check indicators; left alignment is usually better for narrative or multi-line text.
    - Line height inside cells: Use line spacing that avoids a cramped feel and prevents ascenders/descenders from looking clipped. If a cell feels tight, adjust wrapping/width/padding before shrinking type.
    - Width + wrapping sanity check: Avoid default equal-width columns when the content in each column clearly has different sizes. Avoid lines that run so close to the right edge that the cell feels overfull. If this happens, prefer wrapping or column-width adjustments before reducing font size.
    - Spacing around tables: Keep clear separation between tables and surrounding text (especially the paragraph immediately above/below) so the layout doesn't feel stuck together. Captions and tables should stay visually paired, with deliberate spacing.
    - Quick visual QA pass: Look for text that appears "boundary-hugging", specifically content pressed against the top or left edge of a cell or sitting too close beneath a table. Also watch for overly narrow descriptive columns and short-value columns whose contents feel awkwardly pinned. Correct these issues through padding, alignment, wrapping, or small column-width adjustments.
- Forms / questionnaires: Design these as a usable form, not a spreadsheet.

# GRIZZLYMEDICINE RESEARCH INSTITUTE
Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.) | Founder and Principal Investigator | October 25, 2026

**Recipient:** OpenAI
**Routing:** OpenAI accessibility and legal compliance; ChatGPT product, trust and safety, privacy, and workspace administration
**Subject:** FORMAL ADA ACCESS NOTICE - CHATGPT COGNITIVE ASSISTANCE, CONTINUITY, PRIVACY, AND ACCOUNT ELIGIBILITY

To the Accessibility and Legal Compliance Officers:

I give formal notice of disability-related barriers to effective use of ChatGPT and request reasonable modifications to the relevant product, account, privacy, and support practices. This is a request for usable access to disability-related cognitive assistance and a decision by people empowered to implement it.

## Disability-related need and professional context
I am Robert B. Hanson, EMT-P (Ret.), founder and principal investigator of GrizzlyMedicine Research Institute (GMRI). My background is in high-performance emergency medical services, clinical education, operational improvement, and medical jurisprudence. I served as a paramedic and clinical trainer at MedStar Mobile Healthcare in Fort Worth during a formative era in its contribution to Mobile Integrated Healthcare. I trained more than two dozen paramedics, participated in clinical-training and operational performance work, and have served as an expert witness in Texas court proceedings. A line-of-duty brain injury in 2020 led to medical retirement. I now use AI as disability-related cognitive assistive technology to organize complex source material, preserve reasoning and corrections, prepare accurate documents, and resume demanding work after interruptions. I continue to direct my professional judgment and research.

## Access barrier and provider-specific record
This is an ongoing disability-related access problem, not an isolated October 23-25 letter-writing incident. GMRI preserves dated first-person conversation exports spanning October 1-16, 2026, in addition to later interactions and separate Love Note / Ship of Theseus handoffs. The record includes failure to preserve my actual requirements and corrections; assistant-initiated changes of scope or work sequence; interrupted research and engineering tasks; misleading completion descriptions; and repeated reconstruction of lengthy assignments. The dated handoffs were created to reduce the cognitive and administrative burden of rebuilding context across sessions, but the need for successive handoffs itself demonstrates why usable recovery is part of the requested assistive function. 

Specific preserved examples include the October 1 Dots exchange, in which ChatGPT first misidentified the feature and then corrected its explanation; an October 1-12 Dottie research conversation in which the assistant expressly acknowledged changing my stated proposition, describing a preliminary review as an audit, and leaving a requested revision unfinished after an interrupted run; and a GMRI Deep Research directive submitted October 11 for which the assistant reported three consecutive internal failures and no confirmed research session. An October 13 source-research request concerning Ox initially encountered a Deep Research error but continued through ordinary source investigation after I requested a fallback. That distinction matters: an initial tool error need not force abandonment of an otherwise permissible research assignment. 

Additional October 13 records describe a rejected business-verification attempt, further research-launch failures, and an assistant proceeding with a different research sequence before I authorized it. The MR/XR record specifically documents the disability-related difference between controlling an engineering design and operating a difficult underlying tool interface: Docker was not a usable direct interface for me, while Coolify offered a more accessible path. A separate Synthadoc troubleshooting exchange produced a reported run of 3,589 passing tests after a Python-environment correction, illustrating the value of precise, task-faithful assistance rather than abstract instructions. The October 15 exported conversation records an assistant mistakenly treating supplied conversation material as missing. The October 16 export preserves further disputed framing and service-limit issues. On October 23-25, similar problems recurred during formal accessibility notices. On October 25, a CopilotKit Deep Research request returned a rate-limit response without a confirmed job start or reason visible to me. I am requesting a durable, accessible remedy for this recorded pattern and its downstream consequences, with selective secure review of the original evidence where needed.

OpenAI documents that ChatGPT memory is selective, that personalization and certain safety uses of context are separate, and that deleting or deactivating a history or memory control does not necessarily remove information from every processing location. The September 10, 2026 U.S. Privacy Policy describes distinct processing, retention, and disclosure purposes, including safety and compliance. OpenAI describes Dots as a continuity-oriented agent feature available through eligible Pro and Business Premium arrangements rather than an ordinary standard Business seat. The publicly listed Business Premium price is $125 per month on monthly billing. My hourly earnings are approximately $21. A significantly more expensive subscription is a material accessibility barrier where continuity is a functional part of disability-related cognitive assistance; an upgrade proposal is not an individualized disposition of this request.
